votes.reason: The two implementations return different VALUES for the same input, not different labels for the same value. A returns a rung list of length 2 that reaches the target level 12 with a finite total cost of 30; B returns a rung list of length 1 that never reaches the target and a total cost that is not finite. A caller comparing costs sees 30 versus no-finite-cost, and a caller asking "can this character reach level 12" gets yes from A and no from B. That is a difference in the value the function denotes, squarely on the "value semantics" dimension of the declared alphabet — not naming, not field labels, not internal structure, not the ordering of an unordered collection, not formatting. The rung sequence is ordered and differs in length, so no reordering interpretation collapses them. The underlying cause is a genuine semantic choice the spec must settle: whether the projected character state advances derived attributes (max HP) as levels are gained during the walk, or advances only the level counter. That choice flips the S-009 beatability predicate at rung 2 (max_hp 105 > 104 versus 100 <= 104), which in turn flips a finite cost into termination under S-012.

The divergence lives squarely inside the artifact under test. The spec's carve-out for the beatability predicate is explicitly narrow: it excludes only *how it decides*, and expressly retains "when and with what arguments the oracle consults it" as in-scope. A and B use the identical predicate with the identical rule; they differ only in the character state the oracle hands it at rung 2 (max_hp=105 vs 100). That is an argument-construction choice, which the spec reserves to the oracle.

The rung walk — threading a projected state forward across levels, selecting per rung (S-011), stopping when nothing is admissible (S-012) — is entirely the oracle's own machinery. No caller, dependency, or sibling could make this choice: the progression core only consumes rungs and totals, the pricer is never called, and the learning store only supplies observations (empty here). An implementer of this one function must decide whether the walk advances attributes, and nothing in the document tells them.

The "+5 max HP per level" line sits under Domain facts, which are declared "inputs to the specification, not clauses" — that fixes the magnitude but not whether the walk applies growth to its own mid-walk projection. S-009 constrains only the HP *fill* (judge from full HP, not mid-damage) and is silent on whether the ceiling being filled has grown. B is therefore not a strawman: S-002 presents the character state as a given input and no clause directs the oracle to synthesize a successor state.

No residual covers it — the four recorded silences are the XP curve, non-combat routes, catalogue completeness, and deaths — so it is not a declared undecided either. The divergence is visible in the spec's own output vocabulary (S-003 rungs; S-012 not-finite total): two rungs/cost 30 versus one rung/not finite.

The quote is verbatim (SPEC.md Domain facts, lines 46-47, modulo the spec's own line wrap), and no clause in the document settles whether the walk advances the character's ATTRIBUTES (not just its level) as rungs are crossed. The Domain facts section is explicitly labelled "inputs to the specification, **not clauses**"; the "does not get to choose them" phrase forbids substituting different values, not omitting a fact from the projection. The structural proof that facts are not self-binding is S-007: the spec had to write a dedicated clause to make the published XP formula binding, and wired max-level-50 in via S-002 and the 100-turn rule in via the background beatability predicate — but wired the +5 max HP / +2 inventory slots fact in nowhere (the +2 slots half is consumed by no clause at all). S-009 is the near miss and does not close it: "judged from full hit points" fixes current_hp := max_hp but is silent on whether max_hp itself grows, so B still judges from full HP, which is just 100. S-002 enumerates the INPUT state's fields, not a state-transition function; S-003/S-005/S-011/S-012/S-013 govern output shape, cost accounting, selection and stopping, never the advance step. The RESIDUALS list (XP curve, non-combat routes, catalogue completeness, deaths) does not record this silence either. Arithmetic confirms genuine observable divergence: rung 1 = Round(((1/10)x20 + 250x0.04)x0.7) = 8 XP/kill, ceil(100/8)=13 kills x (1 fight + 1 recovery) = 26; at rung 2 cyclops needs max_hp >= 105, so A (max_hp 105 at level 11) crosses for cost 1 + ceil(104/50) = 4, total 30, while B (max_hp still 100) has no earning admissible monster and reports NOT FINITE. One minor flaw in the witness's narrative, not fatal: under B the stop is under S-013 (gingerbread still satisfies S-009/S-010 at level 11 but awards zero at a 10-level gap), which routes reporting through S-012 — the reported output is identical either way. No clause forbids B, so it is a second legal reading rather than a violation, and it flips total cost between finite and not-finite.

NOTE: no spec file path was actually supplied in my task text, so I judged strictly on the clause background restated in the witness (S-005/S-007/S-009/S-012/S-013 as quoted) and read nothing on disk.

This is a real gap, and of the severe kind rather than a don't-care.

1) The spec as restated carries a projected character state that includes max_hp/attack (the S-009 beatability predicate reads max_hp and monster attack directly), and it defines a rung walk that advances the character's LEVEL. It never says what happens to the OTHER fields of that state when a rung is credited. Both readings are faithful to the letter: A advances derived attributes with the level, B advances only the level. That silence is a behavioral hole, not a stylistic one.

2) The outcomes differ in KIND, not degree. A returns a finite plan (cost 30, two rungs). B returns NOT FINITE and stops the walk at rung 1 under S-012. That is the difference between "this objective is reachable and cheap" and "this objective is unreachable" — the most decision-changing output this component produces. An infinite price removes the target from ranking entirely, so the character never pursues level 12 and visibly stalls. Nothing errors; the walk quietly stops one rung early, which makes it painful to diagnose.

3) The failure is asymmetric and silently wrong in the real world. Real characters gain max HP on level-up, so B systematically under-reports reachability wherever beatability hinges on a stat the walk froze (here a 1-HP margin: 100 <= 104 < 105). That is the classic wall shape — a genuinely available route priced at infinity. Conversely, if the intended semantics really are "attributes frozen", an implementation doing A over-promises plans the character cannot execute and burns live cycles on an unwinnable fight. Neither direction is harmless, so this is not a carve-out anyone would shrug at.

4) The spec is doubly silent: it does not say WHETHER attributes advance, and it gives no growth rule. The "+5 max HP per level" in A is a number the witness supplies, not one the quoted background contains — so even an implementer who correctly decides "yes, advance them" has nothing to compute from. Under this project's own API-data-or-fail rule, that second hole is arguably the more damaging one.

Fix: state explicitly which fields of the projected state each rung mutates, and source any per-level attribute growth from game data rather than a constant — or, if attributes are deliberately frozen, say so and accept that beatability is evaluated at input stats throughout. Blast radius 5/5 is defensible; I would not argue it below 4.

- B: ceil(200 / 21) = 10 kills x 2 actions = 20.

Because the measurement (25) and the prediction (3) for chicken differ by ~8x, the choice does not merely perturb the cost; it flips the argmax between candidates (25/action vs 10.5/action under A, 3/action vs 10.5/action under B). So the silence is load-bearing: it changes both the selected element and the reported cost.

S-008 addresses the oracle in the subject position ("the oracle **may** use that measured rate in place of the predicted one"), in the same register as the plainly in-scope S-007. The "may" leaves the measurement-exists branch free while the spec pins the other branch ("Where no measurement exists, S-007's prediction stands"), so the freedom is real and one-sided.

None of the carve-outs absorb it. The learned-observations bullet excludes only "the learning store's collection machinery — how observations are recorded, windowed, or aged," and expressly keeps reading them in scope ("This oracle *reads* observations; it does not produce them"); the witness turns on consumption, not collection. S-007 is conditional ("Where the oracle must predict..."), constraining HOW to predict, never WHEN a measurement must displace prediction — under B the oracle always predicts, which S-007 fully permits. The arithmetic confirms observable divergence under the Domain-facts formula: chicken at gap 9 takes the 70% penalty -> Round(4.4 x 0.7) = 3; cow at gap 2 takes 100% -> Round(20.8) = 21. A ranks chicken 25/1 = 25 over cow 21/2 = 10.5 -> ceil(200/25) = 8 kills x 1 action = total_cost 8. B ranks cow 10.5 over chicken 3/1 = 3 -> ceil(200/21) = 10 kills x 2 actions = total_cost 20 (S-014 round-up applied). The two outputs differ in the monster named on the rung and by 2.5x in total cost, both inside the S-003 output shape. Neither is a violation; the spec simply does not decide.

REAL. The two branches are not two acceptable renderings of the same intent — they are two different answers to "does evidence beat the model?", and the spec's permissive "may use a measurement" answers it neither way.

Verified the witness end to end (numbers reproduce exactly): chicken predicts 3 xp/kill by S-007 but was MEASURED at 25; cow predicts 21 and has no measurement. Branch A (use the measurement) ranks chicken 25/action over cow 10.5/action and returns total_cost 8. Branch B (prediction always stands) ranks chicken at 3/action, loses to cow, and returns total_cost 20. Same input, same admissibility filter, both faithful to the spec.

Why an operator files a bug: the divergence is not a rounding difference in a reported number, it is a different route the character actually executes and a cost that is wrong by 2.5x.
- Observable in the world, not just the log. Under B the bot walks to cows and spends 20 actions killing level-8 monsters while sitting on its own recorded proof that chickens pay 8x better than predicted. Any operator watching the plan tree sees "measured chicken = 25 xp/kill" in one pane and "grind cows" in the other, and that is a bug report with a screenshot attached.
- The prediction is off by 8x here, which is the whole reason to collect measurements. A spec that funds an observation store and then leaves it optional to read has made its most valuable input inert; B is a legal implementation in which every measurement ever taken changes nothing.
- The cost leaks upward. total_cost is what a ranking objective compares across candidate routes, so an 8-vs-20 swing on one rung reorders which goal is pursued at all — the error is not contained to this ladder, it silently changes global route selection.
- It is not a don't-care carve-out. A don't-care is where both outcomes are equally defensible and nobody complains; here one branch demonstrably contradicts observed reality, so there is a right answer the spec simply failed to state.

Worse than binary: "may" also admits the middle readings a coding agent will invent unprompted — use a measurement only above N samples, only if recent, or blend it with the prediction. So the spec does not merely fail to pick between A and B, it fails to bound the space, and no acceptance test derived from it can pin the outcome.

Fix is one clause: state whether a measured rate supersedes the S-007 prediction, and if supersession is conditional, state the condition (sample count, recency, and what happens to catalogue entries that have no measurement — the asymmetry in this very input, where chicken is measured and cow is not, is exactly the case the spec must name).

Blast radius: I would call it 4/5 rather than 5/5 — it corrupts route selection and cost estimates persistently and is user-visible, but it does not lose data, double-charge, or cross a tenant boundary.

votes.reason: A and B return different values for the same input, not different descriptions of one value. A returns an empty rung sequence and a total cost that is not finite (level 13 unreachable); B returns a one-element sequence [L12->L13 via ogre] with total cost 9. No relabelling, reformatting, or reordering of an unordered collection maps one onto the other, and any consumer asking "can I reach 13, and at what cost" gets opposite answers. In scope, and squarely so. The spec's own carve-out for the beatability predicate reads: "Clauses below constrain *when and with what arguments* the oracle consults it, never *how it decides*." A and B run the identical predicate with identical internals; they differ only in the character state passed to it (worn attack 4 vs. best-equippable attack 50). That is exactly "with what arguments," which the carve-out explicitly reserves to THIS artifact. Three corroborations: (1) S-002 requires the state to carry "what it is carrying and wearing" — carried items are admitted input, so the oracle must decide what role they play; nobody else can. (2) S-009 already fixes one dimension of the consulted state (full hit points, with the rationale that recovery precedes the fight in the executed plan) and is silent on the structurally identical equipment dimension — the same rationale would generalize but is not extended. (3) The Domain facts deliberately import "Equipment carries conditions that must hold for it to be worn, including minimum character level," which is load-bearing only if the oracle reasons about wearability of carried gear. The neighbors excluded as background cannot own the choice: the progression core consumes the oracle's output after the fact, the acquisition pricer is never called, the learning store only supplies observations. Divergence is material — NOT FINITE with zero rungs vs. finite cost 9 — flipping the reachability recoverable from the rungs per S-003. No RESIDUAL covers it (the four declared silences are the XP curve, non-combat routes, catalogue completeness, and deaths).

The quote is verbatim (SPEC.md S-009, lines 131-133) and in context. The spec commits to constraining the predicate's arguments — the background bullet at lines 26-28 says clauses "constrain when and with what arguments the oracle consults it" — and S-009's second paragraph then fixes exactly one argument dimension, hit points ("judged from full hit points"), with a "recovery precedes a fight" rationale. It never fixes the equipment dimension, even though S-002 (lines 68-70) hands the oracle "what it is carrying and wearing" — both loadouts are constructible from the input — and the domain fact at line 50 (equipment has a minimum-level condition) makes the steel_sword legally wearable at level 12. None forbids consulting the predicate with a best-equippable loadout. S-005 is the nearest constraint and it accommodates B rather than forbidding it ("anything else the loop requires" would simply add the equip action to the cost). The "projection and executor never disagree" rationale cannot settle it either, since the executor is declared background (line 29) and its loadout behavior is nowhere stated. The divergence is observable and large: A yields rungs=[] and a non-finite total (ogre needs ceil(500/4)=125 turns against the 100-turn cap of line 48; chicken is 10 levels down so the penalty of lines 44-45 zeroes its reward, stopping the walk under S-013), while B yields one finite rung (ogre awards Round(12/12*20 + 500*0.04)=40 XP, 3 kills to cross 100). Minor caveat that does not change the verdict: B's exact total of 9 assumes the equip itself is uncounted; under S-005 a B-family implementation could report 10 — that perturbs the number, not the empty/non-finite versus one-rung/finite divergence.

REAL gap, and a decision-flipping one — not a don't-care.

What is undetermined: when the pricer consults a character's combat capability to decide which monsters are beatable, the spec never fixes the *loadout* the consultation is done against. Both readings are faithful to every other clause: A evaluates against the gear currently worn (attack 4), B against the best gear equippable from worn ∪ carried, respecting the stated min-character-level domain fact (attack 50, steel_sword's min level 12 ≤ 12, so legally wearable now). Same predicate, same rounding, same selection — the divergence is entirely in the unstated input.

Why a user files a bug: the two outputs are not two acceptable shades of the same answer, they are "impossible" vs "cheap". A returns rungs = [] and a NOT FINITE total; B returns a single rung at cost 9. That is not a ranking wobble — an infinite cost removes the whole combat route from consideration, so the caller either falls back to a materially worse route or reports the target level unreachable. The operator's observable complaint writes itself: "my level-12 character is carrying a level-12 sword in its bag and the bot says it cannot reach level 13." Nobody who understands that carried gear is one action away from being worn accepts A silently. Symmetrically, an auditor handed B without a written rule would ask where the equip step went — cost 9 prices 9 fight-shaped units and zero equip units, which is a second, dependent silence the spec also does not settle (does consulting best-equippable oblige the plan to contain the equip, and does that equip cost anything?).

The instance is also not a contrived corner. It is exactly the shape that arises whenever a character has just crafted or withdrawn an upgrade and has not yet worn it — the ordinary steady state after a craft, not a rare one. Under A the pricer is systematically pessimistic for precisely the characters that just did the work to improve, which is the worst possible time to under-price them; under B it is optimistic about gear it has not yet paid to put on. Either is defensible as a design choice, neither is derivable from the spec, and the choice is worth an unbounded cost difference, so it must be written down.

The don't-care carve-out does not apply: there is no reading under which a caller is indifferent between a finite plan and no plan at all. Severity 5/5 is justified — this silently determines whether an entire acquisition route exists.

Fix the spec by stating, in one clause, which loadout the beatability consultation is evaluated against ("as currently worn" vs "the best loadout equippable from worn plus carried, subject to each item's minimum-level condition"), and — if the best-equippable reading is chosen — whether the resulting route must include, and charge for, the equip step.

witnesses.question: What exactly does a stored observation denominate — XP per kill, or XP per executed action over the whole S-005 loop — and which component of the rate does it replace (the per-kill XP only, the loop length only, or the whole reward-per-unit-cost)?

votes.reason: The two implementations emit different numeric payloads for the same input, not different labels for the same payload. A emits rungs=[(10->11 via cow, cost 16)], total_cost=16; B emits rungs=[(10->11 via cow, cost 8)], total_cost=8. Same rung count, same ordering, same monster, same error behavior (neither errors), same idempotence — the sole difference is the magnitude of an emitted cost, which is squarely value semantics under Sigma. A caller budgeting actions, comparing this ladder against a craft route, or reporting the plan sees 16 vs 8 and can act differently, so the divergence is externally visible rather than internal structure or formatting. The root cause is a genuine spec silence rather than a restatement: the spec fixes THAT the measured rate is used (witness 1's decision is held fixed), but never pins the rate's DENOMINATOR. Reading 25 as XP-per-kill (A) versus XP-per-executed-action over the whole S-005 loop, reconciled to per-kill by multiplying by loop cost 2 (B), are both faithful readings, because the prediction the measurement displaces (21) is per-kill while the cost model (2 actions/kill) is per-action. The two readings differ by exactly the loop-cost factor; it does not cancel and does not vanish for any monster whose whole-loop cost is not 1. One consideration against: if the ladder were only ever used to pick WHICH monster to grind, a uniform rescaling by loop cost could leave the argmax unchanged — but that holds only when every candidate shares the same loop cost, and here total_cost is itself an emitted value that downstream pricing reads directly. Observable on value semantics.

SCOPE lens: in scope. The artifact under test is the oracle itself — the pure function that, given the character state, target, observations and catalogue, returns rungs and total cost. The divergence between A and B is entirely inside that function: both receive the identical input (measured rate for cow = 25), and both compute the oracle's own outputs (rungs, total_cost = 16 vs 8) differently because they interpret that number in different denominators (XP/kill vs XP/executed-action, reconciled by the S-005 loop cost of 2).

The nearest carve-outs do not cover it. "The learning store's collection machinery" is explicitly scoped to *how observations are recorded, windowed, or aged* — production, not consumption; the spec then says outright "This oracle *reads* observations". Reading a value and converting it into the per-kill quantity that S-007's prediction is denominated in is the reader's job, and S-008 assigns that job to the oracle in so many words: "A measured rate and a predicted one must be in the same unit before either is used, and the oracle never compares one against the other across units." That sentence imposes a reconciliation obligation on the oracle while never fixing the incoming denominator — the obligation is in scope, the information needed to discharge it is absent. The acquisition-cost pricer, the beatability predicate, the progression choice core and the planner are all untouched by this divergence (S-009's verdict is held fixed by the witness's own framing, and cow is admissible in both).

Applying the literal test: if I implemented only the oracle, could I make this choice? Yes — it is a line of arithmetic inside the oracle (divide 200 by 25, or by 25×2), and nothing outside the oracle can make it for me. The unit of the *reported cost* is pinned hard by S-004 (executed planner actions) and S-005 (whole loop), which is exactly why the unpinned unit of the *rate* propagates straight into a divergent total_cost — a 2× error in the oracle's headline output, the same class of unit error S-004's own rationale says was previously shipped.

REAL. The quote is verbatim (S-008, lines 123-124) and is a unit-*hygiene* rule, not a unit *declaration*: it demands that measured and predicted rates be in the same unit before use, but never says what unit a measured rate natively arrives in, nor how to convert if it differs. Both candidates satisfy it — A treats the measurement as already per-kill (S-007's denominator) and uses it directly; B treats it as XP per executed action and reconciles to per-kill by multiplying by the S-005 loop cost, so at the point of use the two are in one unit and are never compared across units. Neither is a violation.

Full-spec sweep finds no clause that forbids B. S-004 constrains only *reported costs* (both report action counts, 16 vs 8) and, by making "one action, one unit" the house denominator, arguably favors B rather than banning it. S-005 is honored by both (A multiplies kills by loop cost 2; B uses loop cost 2 as the conversion factor — both report a loop-inclusive rung cost). S-007 fixes only the *predicted* side's unit and is silent on the measured side. S-013's "dividing by a zero rate" is unit-agnostic (under B, 200/25 = 8 actions falls out directly). S-014's round-upward is satisfied by both ceilings. S-011 is inert here — one admissible monster. S-002 admits "a body of learned observations" with no declared structure, and the learning store is explicitly BACKGROUND (lines 23-24), so the oracle only reads observations and cannot itself restate their denomination — the unit must be pinned by this document or nowhere. RESIDUALS does not record this as undecided, and line 15 states "This document is the entire subject matter," so the omission is not a deliberate silence.

The divergence is observable under S-003 (rung cost and total_cost: 16 vs 8) — a systematic 2x mispricing of every projected path, the same unit-confusion class S-004's own rationale (lines 95-96) says already shipped once in this codebase. Caveat noted for transparency: I did not open OBSERVATION.md (only SPEC.md was named), so if that companion declares the measured rate's denominator the gap would be closed there; nothing in SPEC.md itself closes it.

No spec file path was actually provided in my task text, so I could not read the clause verbatim; I judged the gap on the witness's own statement of the surrounding clauses, which is itself the telling evidence. The spec supplies a per-monster \"measured rate\" observation without declaring its denominator, while the neighbouring clauses denominate two different things: S-007 states a predicted yield in XP-per-KILL, and S-005 defines a whole-loop cost in ACTIONS-per-kill. Two adjacent, differently-denominated quantities plus a third that must be reconciled against them, with no stated reconciliation rule, is the canonical shape of a real unit gap.

The user impact is concrete and asymmetric. The two readings differ by exactly the loop cost (2 here): A plans 8 kills / 16 actions, B plans 4 kills / 8 actions for the same 200 XP. These are not two acceptable answers — one of them is a factually wrong forecast of how long the level takes, off by the loop-cost factor. Since this is a planner cost model whose entire job is ranking rungs against each other, a systematic 2x error on measured-rate monsters silently reorders them against monsters priced by the unambiguous per-kill prediction. It is also not self-correcting: the error scales with loop cost, so monsters with expensive loops (travel, rest, heal legs) are mispriced worst — precisely where the choice matters most. An operator watching a grind priced at 8 actions consume 16 would file a bug, and would be right to.

This is not a don't-care carve-out. A genuine don't-care would be two readings producing the same plan, or differing only in an unobservable tiebreak. Here the emitted rungs differ in total_cost by 2x and in kill count, both observable outputs the witness exhibits directly. It is also not rescued by \"the measurement is empirical so it must be right\" — the measurement is right; the denominator attached to it is what the spec never fixes.

Caveat on my confidence: the one thing that would make this fake is if the spec pins the unit elsewhere — e.g. the observation alphabet declares the entry as xp_per_kill, or a clause says a measured rate REPLACES the S-007 prediction in place (which would force the per-kill denominator by substitution). Without the spec text I cannot rule that out. But witness 1's use-the-measurement decision is held fixed and divergence still survives, and the failure mode is a silent 2x mispricing of the planner's core cost, so I resolve this as real rather than uncertain. The fix is one clause: state the denominator of a measured rate, and if it is per-action, state the reconciliation to per-kill.

votes.reason:
Note first: no spec path was actually given in my instructions (only clause IDs S-007/S-012/S-013 are cited), so I read nothing and judged the Σ-membership question purely from the two exhibited outputs, which is all this lens requires.

The divergence is observable on value semantics, and on the most consequential value the function produces. A returns total_cost = 36 with rungs = [('wolf', 36)]; B returns total_cost = NOT FINITE with rungs = []. This is not a naming, labelling, field-structure, or formatting difference, and it is not the reordering of an unordered collection — one output is a finite number, the other is the absence of a finite number, and the rung list differs in cardinality (1 vs 0), not merely in arrangement. Any consumer that compares or sums route costs distinguishes them immediately: A says the level-10→11 rung is reachable via wolf at a definite price, B says the rung is unreachable at any price. If costs are used to rank alternatives, A makes this route eligible and comparable, B eliminates it entirely; the two cannot be reconciled as the same behaviour described differently.

The underlying cause is a genuine semantic fork, not an artifact of description: whether an observation record with kills=0 counts as a measured rate of 0.0 xp/action (B) or as no measurement at all, leaving the S-007 prediction of 14.0 xp/action in force (A). Both readings are self-consistent treatments of a zero-kill record, and each propagates deterministically to a different total. That fork is exactly the kind of silence a completeness check is meant to surface, and its effect is visible in the returned values rather than in any internal detail.

I could not verify against the spec text whether one reading is in fact pinned down, but on the declared lens — is the A/B difference actually observable on a Σ dimension — the answer is unambiguously yes, on value semantics.

SCOPE lens: the divergence lives squarely inside the artifact under test. The "Explicitly NOT under test" list carves out the learning store's *collection machinery* — "how observations are recorded, windowed, or aged. This oracle *reads* observations; it does not produce them." The witness does not touch production, recording, windowing or aging: the record is given, identical in both branches. What differs is the oracle's own READ of it — whether a record with kills=0/xp_total=0/actions_total=4 satisfies S-008's antecedent "the observations contain a measured rate for a monster" (lookup HIT, rate 0.0) or fails it (MISS, so "S-007's prediction stands").

That choice is unambiguously the oracle's to make, and I could make it while implementing only this function: S-008 is a clause about what the oracle does when it consults observations, and the two readings propagate entirely through oracle-owned clauses — S-011's "greatest reward per unit cost" selection, S-013's "every admissible monster awards nothing" stop, S-012's not-finite reporting, S-014's round-up. The observable outputs that diverge (rungs = [('wolf', 36)] with total 36, versus rungs = [] with total NOT FINITE) are exactly the two components S-003 declares as this oracle's output shape. Nothing here belongs to the progression choice core, the acquisition pricer, the beatability predicate (both branches agree wolf is beatable and permitted), the planner, or any consumer.

Nor is it deflected by a residual: the four RESIDUALS cover the per-level XP curve, non-combat routes, catalogue completeness, and deaths — none covers what counts as a measurement. S-008 is a genuine clause of the artifact, not transcribed background, and it is silent on whether a zero-kill record is a measured rate; the difference between "reaches target in 36 actions" and "target unreachable" is the maximally load-bearing consequence of that silence.

CONFIRMED REAL. The quoted text appears verbatim in S-008 (SPEC.md lines 121-127) and the spec never defines what makes something "a measured rate" or a "measurement" — no minimum sample, no requirement that a kill completed, no record shape, no staleness or level-matching rule. S-008 is the only clause touching observations and it presupposes the notion it needs; the RESIDUALS section lists four undecided items and this is not among them, so it is unrecorded silence. No clause forbids B: S-013's second sentence is stated generally, not confined to the level-penalty case that motivates it ("A rung at which every admissible monster awards nothing is not crossable by fighting, and the walk stops there under S-012's reporting rule rather than dividing by a zero rate"), so a zero rate is expressly contemplated and B's output (rungs reported, total not finite) is exactly S-012's reporting rule. S-009/S-010 admissibility is stipulated by the input, S-011 picks the sole candidate either way, and S-001 is not violated because "not finite" is a sanctioned answer, not a could-not-compute sentinel. No clause forbids A either: it is the plain S-007 + S-008-second-paragraph path with ceil(500/14)=36 under S-014. A second, independent route to the same underdetermination sits in the same clause: S-008 says the oracle MAY use a measured rate, so even stipulating that the 0-kill record IS a measurement, both using it and ignoring it are permitted.

Real gap with high user impact. The two readings diverge maximally: A yields a finite 36-action plan, B yields NOT FINITE (target level reported unreachable). The triggering record — kills=0, xp_total=0, actions_total=4 — is a commonplace real-world artifact of an engagement that ended without a completed kill (fled, died, interrupted, run stopped mid-fight), not an exotic input. Under B the state is absorbing: the zero-rate record prices the only admissible route at infinity, so the monster is never selected again, so no kill is ever recorded, so the record never improves — the character stalls at level 10 forever beside a monster it can plainly kill. An operator would file that as a total planner failure. Under A the failure is the mirror and far milder: the optimistic 14.0/action prediction stands and the bot retries, self-correcting the moment one kill lands. So the outcomes are not equally acceptable and this is not an unwritten don't-care. The spec must state whether a record with zero completed kills constitutes a measurement at all, and if it does, whether a measured rate of 0.0 halts the walk (S-013/S-012) or falls back to the S-007 prediction — precisely the case where xp_total/actions_total is arithmetically well-defined (0.0) but semantically empty. Severity is high; I would rate it 4 rather than the claimed 5, since the harm is an absorbing-state livelock and a falsely-unreachable goal rather than data loss, double-charging, or a tenant-boundary leak. Caveat: no spec path was supplied in my brief, so I assessed the divergence from the clause behavior described by the witness and did not (and could not, without searching) verify the spec's silence by reading its text.

witnesses.question: Is an observation keyed by monster alone — so it remains in force at every rung of the walk, overriding the player-level-dependent published formula — or is it scoped to the player level at which it was sampled, so higher rungs count as unmeasured?

votes.reason: The two implementations return different values for the same input, not different descriptions of the same value. A yields a finite total cost of 80 with the target level reached; B yields a non-finite cost with the target not reached. That is a difference in the returned result itself, squarely 'value semantics' in the declared alphabet — a caller comparing outputs (80 vs. non-finite, reached vs. not-reached) sees different data, and any downstream ranking or feasibility decision keyed on that cost flips sign. It is not naming, labelling, field structure, formatting, or ordering of an unordered collection: the rung sequence also differs in content (two rungs vs. one), and even if the rung list were dismissed as internal structure, the scalar total cost and the reached/not-reached outcome remain observably different. The underlying disagreement is a genuine semantic gap about the key of a measurement — monster alone vs. (monster, rung level) — which the spec leaves undetermined, and both readings are defensible on the spec's own terms while producing divergent values.

SCOPE lens: this divergence lives inside the artifact under test. The oracle is "ONE pure function" that takes "a body of learned observations" and returns rungs + total cost, and S-008 is a clause about the oracle itself: "Where the observations contain a measured rate for a monster, the oracle may use that measured rate in place of the predicted one... Where no measurement exists, S-007's prediction stands." Deciding whether a rate sampled at character level 10 counts as "a measured rate for a monster" when pricing the level-11 rung is a read-time lookup/applicability decision the oracle makes on every rung — not something a caller, dependency, or sibling supplies. An implementer of this one function must choose it, and cannot avoid choosing it.

The nearest carve-out does not cover it. The BACKGROUND list excludes "the learning store's collection machinery — how observations are recorded, windowed, or aged. This oracle *reads* observations; it does not produce them." That carve-out is about production; the witness is about consumption. Even granting the store full authority over the record's schema, the oracle still decides whether to key its lookup on monster alone or on (monster, rung level) — and if the record carries no level at all, that itself is a fact the spec never states, leaving the oracle's behavior undetermined either way.

The choice is also load-bearing exactly where the spec is most invested. The domain facts make the level penalty a step function of the character-monster gap, and S-013 exists precisely to stop the walk when the fastest admissible monster earns nothing at ten-plus levels above. A measurement keyed by monster alone silently carries a 70%-penalty rate across the boundary into a rung where the published formula says the reward is zero, defeating S-013; a measurement keyed by (monster, level) lets S-013 fire. The two readings produce total cost 80 versus not finite on the same input — a divergence in S-003's own reported output, from the same clause set, with no other component able to arbitrate.

Not out of scope; the subject is the oracle's own use of its own argument.

REAL. The quoted sentence appears verbatim in S-008 ("Where the observations contain a measured rate for a monster, the oracle may use that measured rate in place of the predicted one.") and genuinely admits both readings; no other clause closes it.

The spec never states what a measurement is keyed by. S-002 admits only "a body of learned observations" with no structure. S-008 names the key as "for a monster," which reads as monster-only (A) — but it never says that key is exhaustive, and the background exclusion ("the learning store's collection machinery — how observations are recorded, windowed, or aged") deliberately puts the record's structure out of scope rather than fixing it. So an implementation that treats a sample taken at character level 10 as not being a measurement applicable to the level-11 rung (B) is not contradicting anything written.

The spec is demonstrably aware that the rate varies with character level — S-007's formula carries the gap-based penalty, and S-013 recites it — yet S-008 never says a measurement must be re-keyed, re-scaled, or invalidated when the rung's level differs from the sample's level. That is the missing sentence.

S-008's "may use" compounds it independently: even granting monster-only keying, use of the measurement is permissive, so declining it at the level-11 rung leaves "Where no measurement exists, S-007's prediction stands" / prediction 0.0, and S-013 fires. B is reachable by two separate legal routes.

Checked every clause for a prohibition on B: S-006 (n/a, below target), S-007 (fallback only), S-009/S-010 (chicken beatable and permitted at every rung by construction), S-011 (choice among admitted monsters — one candidate), S-012 (reporting rule for a stopped walk, which B follows), S-014 (rounding), S-001/S-003/S-004/S-005 (purity, shape, unit, loop). None mentions observation keying or forbids stopping at a rung whose used rate is zero.

Nor does S-013 forbid A, which would have collapsed the ambiguity the other way: its first sentence cites the published penalty as motivation, but the operative rule is "a rung at which every admissible monster awards nothing." Under A the oracle's rate for chicken at that rung is the measured 5.0, so the monster does not award nothing on the oracle's own terms. The spec never says a gap of ten or more is deemed zero regardless of any measurement.

The divergence is material and observable in S-003's declared output: A yields rungs [(10, chicken, 40), (11, chicken, 40)] with total 80 and the target reached; B yields rungs [(10, chicken, 40)] with a non-finite total and the target not reached. Reachability is recoverable from the rungs (S-003), so the two implementations disagree on the headline answer, not on an internal detail. Measurement keying is also absent from the RESIDUALS section, so this is an undeclared silence.

Real gap, and a severe one. (Note: no spec file path was given in my instructions, so I judged the ambiguity strictly on its own stated terms — I did not open any file.)

WHY IT IS NOT A DON'T-CARE. The two readings do not differ by a rounding step; they differ by whether the target is reachable at all. A prices the route at 80 actions and returns a plan; B prices it at infinity, drops the rung, and fires the unreachable clause (S-013). Any consumer that ranks routes by cost (the unified objective) will pick a completely different route — or refuse to act — depending purely on how "a measured rate for a monster" is keyed. That is the largest divergence a projection component can produce.

WHY A USER WOULD FILE A BUG. The level-gap penalty exists to encode the grey-mob rule: at gap 10 the monster yields literally zero xp. Under A, a single sample taken at character level 10 is laundered forward into level 11 and asserts 5.0 xp/action for a monster that in fact gives nothing there. The planner then commits to 40 kills that can never advance the level, and the character grinds a dead rung until it stalls out — the exact livelock class this bot has hit before (held-rung grind livelock, grey skill-xp gate). The operator sees hours of burned API rate budget with no level-up, and the plan display insists the target is 40 kills away, permanently. That is a bug report, and a nasty one to diagnose, because the measured value looks authoritative precisely where it is most wrong. The failure is silent and asymmetric: measurements are only ever sampled at the level the character was actually on, so the stale-key reading systematically overstates the tail of every grind, which is where the wall lives.

The reverse complaint is far milder and self-correcting: under B the planner is merely pessimistic about a rung it has not yet observed, falls back to a prediction it already trusts everywhere else, and either finds another route or honestly reports unreachable. An auditor reading B's output is not misled.

WHAT THE SPEC OWES. It must state the key of a measurement — monster alone, or (monster, character level) — and, if the key includes level, whether an unmeasured level falls back to the raw S-007 prediction or to a prediction rescaled by the observed prediction/measurement ratio at the sampled level (a third defensible behavior neither witness exhibits, which is itself evidence the clause is underdetermined). "Where no measurement exists, S-007's prediction stands" is only well-defined once "exists" has a key.

witnesses.evidence: The cost attributed to a rung counts every action the character must execute to cross it, not only the attacking ones. Recovery the character is forced into by the damage it takes counts; so does anything else the loop requires. A monster that must be recovered from after every kill is more expensive per kill than one that can be fought consecutively, and the reported cost must distinguish them.

votes.reason: The two outputs are not the same value dressed differently — they are different values on the same input. A returns rungs = [(10->11, moss_slug, 13)] with total cost 13; B returns [(10->11, steel_golem, 11)] with total cost 11. Both the monster selected for the rung and the numeric cost differ, and cost is expressed in the same unit in both (actions: A = 13 kills = 13 actions; B = 9 kills + 2 recoveries = 11 actions), so 13 vs 11 is a genuine numeric disagreement, not a units/labelling artifact. This is not naming, field labels, formatting, internal structure, or ordering of an unordered collection: the rung list has exactly one element in each, so ordering is not in play, and any caller reading `chosen_monster` or `total_cost` sees a different answer. Both readings are internally consistent and self-justifying — A charges one recovery action after every kill that costs HP; B amortizes recovery over the HP pool (156 HP absorbs three 40-damage fights, so 1.33 actions/kill). Arithmetic checks out on both sides (A: ceil(300/24)=13 for the slug, and the golem would price at 9 kills + 9 recoveries = 18, so the slug wins; B: ceil(300/36)=9 golem kills, recoveries after fights 3 and 6, so 11, and the golem's 27 xp/action beats the slug's 24). So the divergence traces to a real silence in the spec — how the grind loop charges HP recovery, per-damaging-kill versus amortized against the HP pool — which flips both the selected monster and the reported cost. That lands squarely on value semantics, the dimension the witness named, and it is inside Σ. Not error taxonomy (neither errors), not idempotence, not ordering.

SCOPE: in scope. The artifact under test is the cycle oracle itself, and the divergence is entirely inside two things the oracle alone computes: (a) the cost attributed to a rung, and (b) which monster is chosen for that rung. Both are the direct subject of load-bearing clauses — S-005 ("The cost of a rung counts the whole combat loop"; "Recovery the character is forced into by the damage it takes counts... Applying the literal test — "if I implemented the artifact under test, could I even MAKE this choice?" — the answer is yes, and only I can make it: when the walk stops at rung zero I must write *some* value into the total_cost field, and nothing in S-003, S-012, S-013 or S-014 says whether that value is a float infinity, an explicit non-numeric marker (None/sentinel/variant), or anything else. S-014 ("cost is reported as a whole number of actions... resolved upward") governs finite costs and says nothing about the not-finite case; S-013 says only that the oracle must not report "an unbounded cost as though it were a number", which rules out a large finite integer but does not choose between `inf` (which IS a float, and orders and arithmetics silently) and a non-numeric absence.

The witness's TypeError illustration is framed through a consumer, and the consumers — the progression choice core, the planner, the goal layer — are explicitly BACKGROUND ("Explicitly NOT under test"). But the consumer here is only the *detector*, not the *locus*, of the divergence: it is the instrument that makes two different oracle return values observable. The thing that differs between implementation A and implementation B is the oracle's own emitted field, computed inside the artifact, before any background component sees it. That is not a gap in somebody else's code; the choice belongs to this function. Had the witness instead claimed the gap was "the progression core doesn't say how it handles an infinite cost", that would be out of scope — it does not, and the observation stands on this spec's own silence about what its own output carries.

Note also that the spec cannot deflect this to a shared/inherited type: S-003 is where output shape is specified, it defines the total-cost field in prose only ("the sum of those rungs' costs"), and it takes trouble to constrain the output's structure elsewhere ("No second, independently-computed encoding of reachability is produced"). A spec that legislates output structure that carefully, and then leaves the representation of its own most consequential edge value undetermined, is silent on a matter it has already claimed as its own.

VERBATIM: the quoted sentence appears exactly in S-012 (lines 158-159): "The oracle reports the rungs it did cross, and reports the total cost as **not finite** — the target was not reached and no number of actions is claimed to reach it." Nothing in the quote or elsewhere pins a REPRESENTATION for "not finite"; it states a property only.

WHOLE-SPEC SEARCH for a clause that settles it — none does:
- S-003 (output shape) names "a total cost, the sum of those rungs' costs" but declares no type, no encoding, and no representation of the non-finite case; it only forbids a SECOND independent reachability encoding, which neither A nor B adds.
- S-014 says "Cost is reported as a whole number of actions" — this discriminates nothing here, since neither float('inf') nor None is a whole number; S-012 is the more specific clause and explicitly exempts the stopped walk. So S-014 forbids neither A nor B.
- S-001 forbids "a sentinel meaning 'could not compute'". Under B, None does not mean "could not compute" — the oracle DID compute, and the computed answer is "unreachable", exactly the genuine-answer framing S-006 uses for zero and S-012 uses for not-finite. So S-001 does not forbid B. (It equally would not forbid A; float('inf') is no less sentinel-shaped.)
- S-013's "rather than dividing by a zero rate or reporting an unbounded cost as though it were a number" is the only near-miss, and it cuts against A, not B — so even on the reading most hostile to the witness it cannot make B illegal. And it does not cleanly forbid A either: math.isfinite(float('inf')) is False, so inf is the standard engineering encoding of "not finite", and the clause's contrast is plainly with fabricating a finite figure by dividing by a zero rate, not with the IEEE non-finite value.

DIVERGENCE IS OBSERVABLE AND CONSEQUENTIAL — I reproduced it in my own throwaway script (/tmp/witness_probe_9271.py): for the given input (level 10 → target 11, empty catalogue, zero rungs crossed), A yields min(total_cost, 500) == 500 silently, B yields "TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'". A downstream ranker comparing candidate costs therefore either silently prices an unreachable target at a finite bound or crashes — a behavioral difference at the consumer boundary, not a cosmetic one.

Both A and B satisfy every clause as actually written; the spec fixes the property ("not finite") and leaves the representation open. Note one caveat outside my permitted reading: SPEC.md line 3 delegates the observation alphabet to OBSERVATION.md, which I was not authorized to open — if that document declares total_cost's type, the residual could be closed there rather than in SPEC.md.

CAVEAT FIRST: no spec path was supplied in my task, so I could not verify that the spec is in fact silent here — I judged the stated divergence only. If the spec anywhere says the cost of a zero-rung walk "is infinite" (rather than merely "not finite"), A is pinned and this collapses to a non-gap.

On the divergence as stated, this is not a don't-care. inf and None are not two spellings of the same answer; they put the consumer on two different code paths, and the spec's own example shows it: min(total_cost, 500) returns 500 under A and raises TypeError under B. Every downstream use of total_cost is affected the same way — sorted(routes, key=...) works under A and dies on the second comparison under B; a weighted score cost*w is a number under A and a TypeError under B; a JSON/TUI serializer emits `Infinity` (invalid strict JSON) under A and `null` under B. total_cost is the ranking key of the objective, so the blast radius genuinely is "every consumer", which supports the claimed 4/5.

Both outcomes are bug-report material, which is exactly why the silence is load-bearing rather than benign:
- Under A the failure is the dangerous one. An unreachable target — catalogue empty, or every monster failing S-009/S-010 — is priced at inf, then any clamp, cap, normalization, or blend silently converts it to a finite, often COMPETITIVE number. A route that cannot be walked at all then outranks routes that can, and the planner commits to a goal it can never satisfy. That is silent decision corruption of the ranking, and it presents to the operator as a stall/livelock with no error anywhere — the hardest class of bug to attribute, and one this planner has hit repeatedly.
- Under B the failure is loud but still a bug: a plain unreachable-target query crashes the ranking path with a TypeError from inside a min()/sort(), i.e. a normal, expected input takes down the caller.

An implementer reading the spec must choose, an auditor reviewing either choice can point at a concrete misbehavior, and a consumer author cannot write correct code without knowing which. The spec needs to state the sentinel explicitly (and, if inf, state that consumers must test for non-finiteness BEFORE any clamp/blend, since clamping is where the unreachability is destroyed).

witnesses.evidence:
Where two monsters are exactly equal the choice is unconstrained, but it must be
deterministic (S-001) and must not depend on how the monsters happen to be named.
witnesses.distinguishing_input: char = {level: 10, xp_into_level: 0, xp_per_level: 90}, target = 11. Catalogue (both beatable and permitted): wolf = 10 xp/kill, 2 actions/kill; bear = 50 xp/kill, 10 actions/kill. Both are EXACTLY 5 xp per action — an exact tie under S-011's stated ratio.
witnesses.output_a: rungs = [(level 11, "bear", 20)], total cost = 20. (A breaks the exact tie toward the larger per-kill reward: deterministic, and not name-derived, so it satisfies S-011/S-001. ceil(90/50)=2 kills x 10 = 20 actions.)
witnesses.output_b: rungs = [(level 11, "wolf", 18)], total cost = 18. (B breaks the same exact tie toward the cheaper loop: equally deterministic and non-name-derived. ceil(90/10)=9 kills x 2 = 18 actions.)
witnesses.recommended_default: S-011 declares the tie "unconstrained" on the assumption that an exact ratio tie means the outcomes are interchangeable — under S-014's upward rounding they are not, because the loser's last kill overshoots by a different amount, so the TOTAL COST the oracle reports differs. Either (a) adopt witness 1's argmin-on-rung-cost selection, which dissolves this tie into a comparison on the quantity that is actually reported, and then break any residual tie on the smaller per-kill loop cost, or (b) keep the ratio argmax but mandate the tie-break explicitly (smallest loop_cost, then smallest xp_per_kill) and delete the word "unconstrained" — a free choice here is a free choice of the number the ranking core consumes.
witnesses.cell: 11. Fastest-monster selection (argmax on reward per unit cost) and tie-break/conflicting
witnesses.question: When two monsters have exactly equal reward per unit cost but different rung-crossing costs, which specific deterministic, non-name-derived key breaks the tie (cheaper loop, larger per-kill reward, higher/lower monster level)?

votes.reason:
Σ-membership holds. The two outputs are not the same behavior relabelled: A returns rungs = [(11, "bear", 20)] with total cost 20; B returns rungs = [(11, "wolf", 18)] with total cost 18. The total-cost field is a number that a caller reads and compares, and it differs — 20 vs 18. That is squarely "value semantics", the first dimension of the declared alphabet, and it is the dimension the witness named.

The difference is not naming, not field labels, not internal structure, and not ordering of an unordered collection: the rung list has one element in each case, so there is no permutation story available, and the differing element carries both a different monster identity (which monster the character is actually directed to fight — plan content, not a display label) and a different action count. Nothing here is a formatting artifact.

The interesting part, and why the divergence is substantive rather than cosmetic, is that the tie is real at the selection key but does NOT propagate to the cost: both monsters are exactly 5 xp per action, so any rule phrased purely as "maximise xp per action" (S-011's stated ratio) leaves the choice free — yet the two choices do not cost the same, because the kill count is integral. ceil(90/50) = 2 kills of bear rounds up and wastes 10 xp of overkill (2 x 10 = 20 actions), while ceil(90/10) = 9 kills of wolf divides evenly (9 x 2 = 18 actions). The ceiling breaks the ratio tie into a strict cost inequality. So a spec that ties only on the ratio, and demands merely that the tiebreak be deterministic and not name-derived, admits both A and B while they emit different numbers — exactly the shape of an underdetermined clause, not a described-two-ways equivalence.

Judged as Σ-membership alone, and setting aside whether some other clause might independently force minimisation of total actions: the observable outputs differ on value semantics, so this is real.

In scope. The divergence is entirely internal to the artifact under test — the cycle oracle's own per-rung monster selection (S-011) and its own cost rounding (S-014), producing different values for outputs the oracle itself is required to return (S-003 rungs and total cost). No caller, dependency, or background component is involved in the causal path: the oracle is the only thing that picks the rung's monster and the only thing that converts that pick into a rounded action count, so an implementer of this function must make the choice and cannot delegate it. The "Explicitly NOT under test" list does not cover it: the progression choice core's excluded tie-breaking is over the oracle's *results* at a different layer, the beatability predicate carve-out covers only *how* it decides (S-009/S-010 admissibility is unchallenged here — both monsters are stipulated beatable and permitted), and the pricer, learning store, planner and non-combat concerns are untouched. The only clause resembling a carve-out is S-011's own "where two monsters are exactly equal the choice is unconstrained," but that grants freedom *within* this artifact rather than assigning the subject to another one — and the witness's point is that the freedom is not observationally free, since ceiling rounding (S-014) makes an exact ratio tie diverge in reported cost (ceil(90/10)x2 = 18 vs ceil(90/50)x10 = 20). This silence is also not among the four items the RESIDUALS section records as deliberately undecided.

The quoted sentence appears verbatim in S-011 (lines 152-153): "Where two monsters are exactly equal the choice is unconstrained, but it must be / deterministic (S-001) and must not depend on how the monsters happen to be named." In context, "exactly equal" is scoped by the immediately preceding sentence's criterion — "the greatest reward per unit cost, in the unit S-004 fixes and over the whole loop S-005 describes" — so wolf (10 xp / 2 actions) and bear (50 xp / 10 actions) are exactly equal at 5 xp per action and land squarely inside the grant of freedom.

The defect is that the grant is written as though a ratio tie were cost-indifferent, which S-014's upward rounding makes false. S-014 requires a fractional intermediate figure to be resolved upward, so bear needs ceil(90/50) = 2 kills = 20 actions while wolf needs 90/10 = 9 kills = 18 actions. The tie in the ranking key therefore does NOT produce a tie in the reported output: S-003 defines the total as the sum of the rungs' costs, and each rung's cost is whatever the chosen monster's loop costs (S-005), so "unconstrained" choice leaks directly into an observable difference in both the rung's named monster and the total cost (20 vs 18).

I checked every clause for something that forbids B (wolf/18) and found nothing. S-001 (both rules are deterministic and neither is name-derived), S-003/S-004/S-005 (shape and unit only), S-006 (character is below target), S-007/S-008 (both rates are catalogue/observation-derived), S-009/S-010 (both stipulated beatable and permitted), S-012/S-013 (a monster exists and both award nonzero xp), and S-014 (both totals are whole numbers resolved upward) all admit B. The only text pulling toward a unique answer is S-011's *heading*, "the one that crosses it fastest" — and that reading, if anything, favors B (18 < 20) and would forbid A; it cannot forbid B. The heading is also explicitly qualified by the clause body, which defines the criterion as the ratio and then hands ties over as unconstrained. So both A and B are legal readings of the text as written, with no clause resolving which, and the spec is silent on whether ties must be broken toward minimal rung cost.

Real gap. The two implementations do not merely pick different internal representatives of an equivalent class — they emit different values of the primary observable output: the rung's monster name AND the total cost (20 vs 18). Anything downstream that consumes the number (a route price, a plan display, a comparison against a non-grind route) sees a materially different answer, so this is observable divergence, not a hidden don't-care.

Why a user/auditor files a bug: the function's whole purpose is "cheapest path to level." Implementation A returns 20 actions when an 18-action path over the same permitted, beatable catalogue demonstrably exists. That is a self-falsifying output — an auditor reading "cheapest" in the name/contract and seeing a provably non-minimal cost will file it, and be right to. There is no reading under which "return a 10% more expensive path than one you already enumerated" is an acceptable alternative outcome; it is not symmetric with B, where nobody can point at a cheaper path.

The root of the gap is exactly what the ambiguity name says: the ratio is a *proxy* that is not cost-indifferent once the kill count is ceilinged. ceil(90/50)=2 wastes 10 xp of overshoot; ceil(90/10)=9 wastes none. So equal xp-per-action does NOT imply equal actions-to-target, and any tiebreak keyed on something other than the realized ceilinged cost can return a non-minimal answer. S-011 as quoted ranks on the ratio and S-001 only demands determinism and non-name-derivation — both A's "prefer larger per-kill reward" and B's "prefer cheaper loop" clear those bars, so the spec genuinely fails to determine the output.

Severity: no data loss, double-charge, or cross-tenant leak, so not top-severity; but it silently mis-prices a decision input, and mis-pricing is the failure mode this kind of cost function exists to prevent. The claimed 4/5 blast radius is somewhat inflated — an EXACT ratio tie is rare in real catalogue data — but the fix is cheap and the spec text needed is one clause. Recommended clause: after ranking by xp-per-action, break ties by the realized total cost (ceil(remaining_xp / xp_per_kill) * actions_per_kill), and only then by a further deterministic non-name-derived key. Stronger and preferable: rank on the realized ceilinged cost directly and drop the ratio as the primary key, since the ratio and the true cost disagree wherever the last kill overshoots — which is not only at exact ties.
